“Training, huh?
What’s your Dharma name?”
“I have yet to receive one of those as well.”
“So you’re a monk with neither precept seals nor a Dharma name...”
The hulking man muttered under his breath, then let out a short laugh and turned to his subordinates.
“Just going by the packaging, he looks exactly like one of us.
Don’t you think?”
“Yes, sir!”
“He looks like he’d be good at the job.
We should take him in as our youngest.”
“Right?”
The hulking man roared with laughter, then abruptly went stone-faced and glared at the monk.
“Where did you come from?”
“...I’m afraid I don’t understand.”
“I know all about you, you bastard.
I asked where you came from.
The Poison Dragon Sect?
Or the Black Blood Sect?”
“T-the Poison Dragon Sect?
The Black Blood Sect?
This poor monk comes from Shaolin.”
“What?
Shaolin?
Shaolin Temple on Mount Song?”
“Yes.”
Shaolin Temple?
Now this was getting interesting.
Even Jeok Cheongang, who had been ignoring everything happening behind him, turned to watch.
“Old Master, he says he’s from Shaolin Temple.”
“Be quiet.
I’m deciding how to deal with an ill-mannered brat like you.”
That wasn’t good news.
My expression probably looked a lot like the monk’s right about now.
His face had fallen as he stared at the hulking man, who burst into thunderous laughter.
“Ha-ha-ha-ha!
Shaolin Temple?
You’re claiming to be from Shaolin Temple?”
“B-benefactor, why are you laughing?”
“Benefactor, my ass.
Who the fuck is this mangy stray, crawling out of nowhere and spouting bullshit to my face?”
Boom!
The hulking man’s fist shattered the solid wall.
Unlike his subordinates, who were Second or Third Rate at best, he possessed enough martial prowess to pass himself off as a Peak master wherever he went.
Though he had only barely entered the realm.
“You little bastard...
You think our Dongcheon Sect is a joke?
Do I look that stupid to you?”
“Benefactor, you seem agitated.
Please calm yourself.
Settle your heart.”
“Settle my ass!”
Boom!
What remained of the wall crumbled to the floor.
The innkeeper watching from the back probably felt his heart crumble along with it.
“You don’t have the precept seals that should be carved into your forehead, you don’t have a Dharma name, and you look like the perfect dark-path thug, but you expect me to believe you’re a monk?
You little shit.
Why don’t you just tell me the Abbot of Shaolin is your master?”
“Gasp!
How did you know?”
The young monk’s eyes widened.
That was the last straw for the hulking man.
“You son of a—!”
Whoosh!
A mace covered in sharp steel spikes hurtled toward the monk.
It traced a clean, practiced arc worthy of an experienced First Rate master.
With a startled gasp, the monk raised the prayer beads in his hand.
Screams erupted from the crowd watching outside the inn.
“Eek!”
“Look out!”
But what they feared never happened.
Clang!
With a sharp metallic ring, something came raining down.
Astonishingly, the small, pointed objects raining down were the steel spikes that had covered the mace.
The hulking man stared at his mace in confusion.
Then the young monk shouted in a terrified voice,
“Benefactor, you started this!”
“W-wait!”
But the situation had already taken an unexpected turn.
Rattle-rattle-rattle!
The absurdly large prayer beads wrapped around the monk’s entire arm.
The beads threaded between his fingers gleamed with a strangely familiar sheen.
Wait.
Could those be...
Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron?
The realization flashed through my mind just as a horrifying sound rang out.
Crack!
Crunch!
A single punch shattered the mace and drove straight into the hulking man’s side.
“Guh!”
His mouth fell open from the pain, and blood poured from between his lips.
“W-wait!”
The hulking man cried out desperately, but his plea never reached his opponent.
Already white as a sheet, the young monk squeezed his eyes shut and shouted,
“Amitabha!”
Thud!
“Namu!”
Crack!
“Avalokiteshvara!”
Crunch!
“Amitabha, Amitabha, Amitabhaaa!”
Bam-bam-bam-bam-bam!
He hit him, broke him, then struck the places he had already hit again.
Every time the gleaming prayer beads shot forward, blood sprayed through the air.
Watching the scene, I muttered like I was groaning in pain.
“Oh, shit...”
That was the strongest reaction I could muster.
I had expected the monk to win from the moment he appeared, but I had never imagined he would be this insane.
“T-that...”
Jeok Cheongang had shot to his feet at some point.
His mouth hung open.
“The Arhat Fist!”
“Arhat?
As in Shaolin’s Hundred and Eight Arhats?”
“Y-yes.
That is definitely Shaolin martial arts.”
“...That is?”
I looked back.
The young monk’s eyes had half rolled back in his head as he delivered the finishing blow to the fallen man.
“Gate, gate, paragateeek!”
Bam-bam-bam!
The scene was covered in brutal violence and blood.
I wiped the blood from my cheek and barely managed to speak.
“...Old Master.”
“Speak.”
“Is that really Shaolin martial arts?”
“...Technically.”
“Then why can’t I feel even a trace of the Buddha’s compassion or anything like that?”
After a brief pause, Jeok Cheongang gave a short answer.
“At least he didn’t kill him.”
At this point, killing him seemed like it might actually be kinder.
But I swallowed the words before they could escape.
Clink, clink.
The prayer beads swung and rattled with every step.
A blood-drenched robe and a pair of unsteady eyes drew closer.
“Um, excuse me.”
“Yes?”
“Forgive me, but may I ask your name, Benefactor?”
“W-why?”
My voice trembled despite myself.
The young murderer—no, the young monk—edged closer with timid steps.
“Could you perhaps be a member of the Jin family...?”
“I’m sorry.
You have me confused with someone else.”
“That is Jin Taekyung.”
When Jeok Cheongang cut in, I immediately changed my answer.
“That’s right.
I was only joking.
I didn’t offend you, did I?”
“Amitabha.
Of course not.”
Fortunately, he didn’t seem upset.
Unlike me, who kept glancing uneasily at the prayer beads, he wore a joyful smile around his mouth.
If not for the drop of blood splattered beneath his chin, I might have thought, So this is what the smile of a Buddha looks like.
“But why were you looking for me?”
“This poor monk was ordered to bring the Master of Morning Star.”
The master of what?
Before I could ask again, Jeok Cheongang abruptly spoke.
“Do you know Hong Dao?”
“Yes.
He is my master.”
That damned monk is as uncanny as ever.
He can still see a thousand li without leaving his seat.”
“Then you must be the Fire King, Great Hero Jeok Cheongang.”
“Did your master tell you that too?”
The young monk silently bowed his head, and Jeok Cheongang let out a short laugh.
“No need for a lengthy explanation, then.
Take us to Hong Dao.”
“Yes.”
As Yama disguised as a monk led the way, the crowd parted like the Red Sea.
Taking advantage of the renewed commotion, I asked Jeok Cheongang in a low voice,
“Old Master, who is Hong Dao?”
“The Abbot of Shaolin.”
That alone was surprising, but Jeok Cheongang wasn’t finished.
“In the Murim, they call him the Dharma King.”
Unnamed.
That was the Dharma name of the young monk who introduced himself as the Disciple of Dharma King Hong Dao.
Though, technically, it could hardly be called a Dharma name.
It literally meant he had no name.
“He hasn’t changed a bit, even in his old age.
What kind of Dharma name is that to give a Disciple?”
Jeok Cheongang clicked his tongue, and Unnamed smiled sheepishly.
“My master gave it to me, so it is both my name and my Dharma name.”
“From what this old man can tell, you don’t seem to have been formally accepted as his Disciple.
Do you have no regrets about that?”
“Is it not all Heaven’s will?”
Unnamed pointed toward the sky with a bright smile.
Jeok Cheongang shook his head.
“Even when choosing a Disciple, he really...
How should I put this?”
After a moment’s hesitation, he continued,
“He chose an unusual one.”
“Hehe.
Amitabha.
Thank you.”
Don’t laugh.
That wasn’t a compliment.
And stop saying Amitabha.
Even now, whenever I closed my eyes, I could vividly see Unnamed drenched in blood.
When he smiled, he looked like a living Buddha.
But the moment he slipped those prayer beads between his fingers, everything within ten meters turned into a living hell.
This bastard is the scariest one here.
From what I had heard during the half day we’d traveled together, he was so naturally introverted that once he snapped, he couldn’t control himself.
Jeok Cheongang tilted his head a few times before giving a vague nod, but I had a different opinion.
I even knew his exact diagnosis.
Anger-management disorder.
The man was a walking time bomb.
That was why I had been trying to stay behind Unnamed whenever possible.
A Peak master with anger-management disorder could strangle me with those Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron prayer beads.
Getting strangled with prayer beads...
No.
Absolutely not.
Fortunately, the journey from Luoyang to Mount Song didn’t take long.
The two were close to each other, and the roads were well maintained thanks to the many pilgrims who visited Shaolin Temple.
As we reached the foot of Mount Song, wooden buildings began to appear in the distance.
“Are we there?”
Jeok Cheongang shook his head.
“Not yet.
We still have to climb halfway up Shaoshi Peak.
Visitors without a specific purpose are only permitted to stay at the Guest Reception Hall.”
“You know this place well.
Have you been here often?”
“I’ve stopped by often.”
“Oh.”
Well, the Abbot of Shaolin was his friend.
I supposed it was only natural for him to know that much.
Jeok Cheongang dismounted and began climbing Shaoshi Peak.
After a while, he abruptly spoke.
“You haven’t given up that lazy habit, I see.
Do you still sleep five shichen a day?”
The next moment, an unexpected answer came from a broad, flat rock far above us.
It was a presence only a master of Jeok Cheongang’s caliber could have sensed.
“Hmm.
Five shichen.
There was a time when I could sleep that long.”
The voice resembled the tolling of a bell in an ancient temple.
It was quiet yet weighty, with a deep resonance.
“Being the Abbot of Shaolin is a grave responsibility.
I can no longer sleep as much as I used to.”
“Is that so?”
“Of course.
It is a sense of responsibility that a carefree Fire Gate Sect Leader like you could never understand.”
Jeok Cheongang and Hong Dao spoke as casually as if they had seen each other only yesterday.
“So how many shichen do you sleep?”
“Hmm.
Well, you see...”
Whoosh.
A black silhouette slowly descended from the broad, flat rock several dozen meters above us.
Very slowly, stepping on empty air as though it were solid ground, Dharma King Hong Dao landed and smiled like a child.
“Only about four shichen.”
“You lazy bastard.”
A smile tugged at the corners of Fire King Jeok Cheongang’s mouth.

chapters.title: Chapter 232
paragraphs: Unlike the short Jeok Cheongang, Dharma King Hong Dao was a remarkably tall old man.
His eyes sparkled with mischief, and his steps were full of vigor as he climbed the mountain path.
Where are we going, anyway?
It was only natural to wonder. He had abandoned the well-maintained road and was deliberately taking paths hardly anyone ever used.
After walking for some time, Hong Dao finally stopped.
“Humble guests have come to this precious place. I know it may be a burden, but don’t stand on ceremony. Come in.”
Jeok Cheongang stared at the so-called precious place before speaking.
“Did you get kicked out of Shaolin Temple or something?”
“Hm? Why?”
“You really have to ask? What happened to your residence?”

Just as Jeok Cheongang had said, the place was surrounded by thick weeds and trees. It looked far too shabby to be the residence of the Abbot of Shaolin Temple, the Mount Tai and Northern Dipper of the Murim.
“Be honest. You got fired as Abbot of Shaolin, didn’t you?”
Seriously, what was he, a convenience-store part-timer?
Dumbfounded by Jeok Cheongang’s words, I asked, “Can an Abbot even be fired?”
“What a narrow-minded fool. Rebels can depose an emperor, so why couldn’t they do the same to an Abbot of Shaolin?”
When he put it that way, I had nothing to say.
Besides, I used to beat monsters for a living in the modern world. In a world with Demon Kings and Gates, I supposed even the Abbot of Shaolin could be a temporary employee.
Hong Dao, who had been listening to our exchange, chuckled.
“Wherever I am becomes the Abbot’s quarters. We don’t bother with such formalities at Shaolin. Isn’t that right, Disciple?”
Unnamed answered, “He is currently staying here despite the Discipline Hall’s pleas for him to return.”
Like friend, like friend. This old man was no pushover either.
Hong Dao, however, only laughed heartily as he pulled out some kind of staff from inside his robes and waved it around.
“What can they do? They’re the ones who forced the position of Abbot on someone who said he didn’t want it.”
It was a ridiculously short staff. Its surface, polished by countless hands, gleamed as though it had been oiled, and a faint green light shimmered across it.
And there’s some strange-looking stone set into it.
Its shape somewhat resembled the staffs used by mages.
But there was something different about Hong Dao’s green staff. Beyond the marks left by time, it possessed a unique energy all its own.
What is that?
My question was answered the next moment.
“The Green Jade Buddha Staff. To think they entrusted a thousand-year-old sacred treasure of Shaolin, one bearing such immense authority, to a dirty monk like this. They must all be blind.”
Jeok Cheongang clicked his tongue.
“Shaolin is really going downhill.”
“It’s still doing much better than the Fire Gate Clan, which has all of one Disciple.”
“What did you say?”
“Your fiery temper hasn’t changed. I hope you’re reborn as a good and calm person in your next life.”
“My next life? Why are you killing me off when I’m still perfectly healthy?”
“Oh, my. A corpse is talking. Amitabha.”
“Hong Dao, you dirty monk!”
I watched the two of them bicker as they entered the Buddha hall, then turned around.
Unnamed was looking at me with a faint smile.
“They both seem pleased to see an old friend after so long.”
“...I can’t imagine how they ever became friends.”
The eccentric Abbot of Shaolin and the foul-tempered Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.

Their personalities might be a decent match, but they still didn’t seem like the sort of pair who would become friends. Besides, hadn’t Jeok Cheongang killed countless people, despite Buddhism’s prohibition against taking life?
Unnamed thought over my dubious remark, then suddenly smacked his gleaming forehead.
“Ah, I remember now.”
“You startled me. I thought you were about to use Solar Fist... But what did you remember?”
“How they became friends. During the Great Faction War, my master was secretly drinking and eating meat. Benefactor Jeok caught him, and they became drinking buddies afterward.”
“What?”
For a moment, I wondered if I had misheard him.
“He was drinking and eating meat?”
“Yes.”
“Wasn’t he already the Abbot of Shaolin back then?”
“That is correct.”
“Oh, so the monks here eat meat. Well, I suppose they need to bulk up while training in martial arts, so that makes sense...”
“That is not the case. Buddhism forbids taking life. Livestock are no exception.”
Where had this conversation gone wrong?
I stared blankly at Unnamed for a while, unable to say anything more.
Then I looked at the muscles writhing beneath his loose robes and became certain.
This bastard eats meat too.
Just look at those muscles. There was no way he had built a physique like that on temple vegetable bibimbap alone.
He would have to roast an entire pig whenever he got bored, and even his bibimbap would have to be beef-tartare bibimbap.
Shaolin Temple? More like the Temple of Wine Pools and Meat Forests.
Whoever said you couldn’t predict even an inch ahead in the Murim had been absolutely right.
Shaking my head, I followed the others into the Buddha hall.
The interior of the Buddha hall was small and old, but it had an elegant, antique charm.
The floor was spotless, and Buddha statues of every size stood throughout the hall.
Unnamed stepped away for a while, leaving Jeok Cheongang, Hong Dao, and me seated across from one another, emptying our teacups. The tea, brewed from some unknown herb, was bitter and astringent.
“This is no way to treat an honored guest. What is this?”
“What do you think? Tea leaves I grew myself.”
“Tea leaves? You?”
“I’m old enough to know better, so I decided it was time to give up ‘grain tea’ as well. That was decades ago.”
For someone who had supposedly given it up, he seemed to have drunk enough alcohol to last a lifetime.
I couldn’t bring myself to say it aloud and merely tipped my cup back. Jeok Cheongang, on the other hand, gaped at him.
“Are you sick? Do you have some terminal disease?”
“A terminal disease... Perhaps I do, perhaps I don’t. I’m not sure myself.”
His answer was calm, but Jeok Cheongang’s face stiffened.
“Does that mean...?”
“We’ll discuss that later.”
Hong Dao lightly waved a hand to cut him off, then turned and stared intently at me.
“Now, then... Are you the Master of Morning Star?”
The Master of Morning Star.
I had first heard the phrase from Unnamed only half a day ago.
I assumed rumors about a Morning Star appearing in the Murim had spread through the usual gossip.
The rumor has already reached this far?
The name Sleeping Dragon of Shanxi was gaining popularity by the day, but I hadn’t expected even the Abbot of Shaolin to recognize me.
Having suddenly gone world-class, I smiled awkwardly.
“That’s too much praise. I’m not quite at that level yet.”
“You’re more obtuse than you look.”
“Excuse me?”
“Did I not call you the Master of Morning Star?”
Yes, but what does that mean?
Seeing my bewildered expression, Hong Dao smiled faintly.
“Benefactor, do you know what a Morning Star is?”
“Uh, well... Don’t people usually call those who distinguish themselves Morning Stars?”
“And?”
“...A star?”
“Exactly.”
Hong Dao nodded and continued in a calm voice.
“I have observed the heavens for a very long time. Perhaps the effort was not entirely futile, for I eventually learned to see and read the heavenly patterns to some extent.”
“The heavenly patterns...”
The events of the past half day suddenly flashed through my mind.
Unnamed had come looking for us on his master’s orders, and the moment he saw me, he had called me the Master of Morning Star.
And what had Jeok Cheongang said? Ah, right.
What an uncanny dirty monk. He can still see a thousand ri without leaving his seat.
He hadn’t guided us here using information gathered from other people. He had read the heavenly patterns.
If that’s true, he’s far beyond some fake fortune-teller.
Calling it prophecy wouldn’t even be an exaggeration.
I sensed something unusual from Hong Dao and swallowed hard.
“So?”
“A Morning Star is like a firework. It shines brightly in the night sky, then fades with time. But this one was different.”
Hong Dao pointed through the open doors of the Buddha hall, toward the distant north where Shanxi Province lay.
“One day, a new Morning Star rose in the north. Its light has yet to fade. No, it grows brighter with each passing day.”
“People often compare humans to stars. I believe that Morning Star is you.”
Whenever someone is born or dies after accomplishing something great, people rejoice or lament.
A new star has risen. Or a great star has fallen.
But the Morning Star that appeared this time is supposed to be me?
Hong Dao clearly meant it as something good.
Still, I wasn’t sure what to make of it.
Just as I scratched the back of my head with a perplexed expression, one of Hong Dao’s words pierced my ears.
“That was four months ago.”
My entire body tingled as though I had been struck by electricity.
My mouth went dry, and my heart pounded. One thought spun endlessly through my mind.
Four months ago?
If it was then...
That was around the time I had first awakened in the Murim.
Hong Dao smiled warmly at me as I swallowed dryly.
“You seem to have something in mind.”
“N-no. Nothing at all.”
Jeok Cheongang, who had been listening silently, cut in with a disgusted look.
“It’s written all over your face, you idiot.”
“I-it really isn’t.”
“Oh? Shall I rip out that tongue of yours?”
“W-why are you doing this to me?”
Damn it. My tongue wouldn’t stop tripping over itself.
Hong Dao burst into laughter as I slowly edged my bottom away from Jeok Cheongang to avoid his sharp gaze.
“It seems the benefactor is in urgent need of the privy. You may leave.”
“Go on—if you want me to shove you into the latrine.”
I looked back and forth between the two of them, then bolted for the door.
Behind me, I heard Hong Dao’s booming laughter and Jeok Cheongang’s shouts.
“Ha! Ha-ha-ha!”
“What an ill-mannered brat. How dare he run off while his master is speaking...”
Hong Dao looked at the grumbling Jeok Cheongang.
“Is he the Disciple you recently took in?”
Jeok Cheongang flinched and hurriedly cleared his throat.
“Ahem. Kheh-hem! He isn’t my Disciple. He begged and pleaded for me to teach him a thing or two, so I’m merely looking after him for a while. Yes. That’s all.”
“Is that so?”
“I told you it is!”
“If that’s the case, why are you shouting? You’ll anger the Buddhas.”
“Hah. Listen to the way this dirty monk talks.”
Ignoring Jeok Cheongang’s reaction, Hong Dao drained his teacup in one gulp and grimaced.
“Ugh, bitter. Hurry and finish yours.”
“Finish this crap? Why would I drink something so bitter?”
“How can I pour the liquor if your cup isn’t empty?”
“What?”
“I’ve been saving something for a day like this.”
With a sly smile thoroughly unbecoming of a monk, Hong Dao rose and approached the row of Buddha statues.
He effortlessly lifted aside the largest statue, fumbled behind it, and pulled out a small earthenware jar.
“Snake liquor aged for thirty years.”
“Snake liquor?”
“The Thousand-Year Poison Horned Snake. Have you heard of it?”
“The Thousand-Year Poison Horned Snake!”
Jeok Cheongang’s eyes lit up.
He hurriedly opened the tightly sealed jar. Sure enough, the snake inside was larger than a python, with a horn protruding from its triangular head.
A poisonous aura strong enough to make his nose tingle poured from the jar. Jeok Cheongang stared in amazement.
“Isn’t this thing lethally venomous? Where did you catch it?”
Hong Dao gazed off toward the distant mountains.
“While I was out for a walk.”
“...You must have searched the whole mountain with the intention of making snake liquor from the start. There are limits to being a dirty monk. Now you’re killing things just to have a drink?”
“If you don’t want any, never mind. I’ll drink it myself.”
“Now, now.”
Jeok Cheongang gave Hong Dao a pointed glare, then muttered, “Still, this thing’s venom must be no joke...”
“Indeed. A single drop of venom squeezed from a Thousand-Year Poison Horned Snake can kill a hundred cows.”
“It’s been in there for thirty years. At this point, that’s not liquor. It’s poison.”
“We only broke the seal for a moment, and already this much poisonous energy has spread through the air. What more is there to say?”
“Something this strong would kill even a decent master, wouldn’t it?”
“It would be madness to drink it. We absolutely shouldn’t.”
Their gazes met in midair.
Then they spoke almost simultaneously.
“Then we have to drink it.”
“Of course. Absolutely.”
“Surely it won’t kill us.”
“Drink. We’re drinking it no matter what. I read the heavenly patterns, and today isn’t the day we die.”
Both men were over a hundred years old, yet neither could escape the simple recklessness etched deep into every man’s bones.
Before long, they were passing the jar back and forth and guzzling the liquor as though possessed.
Half a shichen later, early darkness had settled over the mountain, and the jar was empty.
“Ooh, that venomous tingle on the tip of the tongue gives it an incredible kick. Thanks to my Scorching Yang Qi, the poison can’t even touch me.”
Jeok Cheongang licked up the very last drop while Hong Dao glared at him.
Though both men numbered among the Ten Kings, a slight difference in skill still existed.
Hong Dao had lost out in the grappling technique they used to wrestle the jar away from each other, so he had not managed to drink even half of what it contained.
“An old brute with nothing but strength. No wonder you’ve lived so long.”
“Were you hoping I’d die?”
“I at least expected you to clutch your stomach and roll around.”
Pleasantly drunk, Jeok Cheongang burst into laughter.
“That’s what the heavenly patterns said, isn’t it? What can you do when Heaven has decided your lifespan?”
“The heavenly patterns...”
Hong Dao murmured the words, then casually added, “That was a lie.”
“Hm? What do you mean?”
“Exactly what I said. I’ve been slowly going blind for the past thirty years.”
“W-wait. Are you saying you can no longer read the heavenly patterns?”
Hong Dao nodded silently, and Jeok Cheongang’s heart sank.
“How did it happen? Is it because of your age?”
“At first, I thought so too. But I was mistaken. I gave up the liquor I loved so much and secluded myself in the wilderness to calm my mind, yet nothing changed.”
“Then...”
“It isn’t because this old man’s faculties have grown dull.”
Hong Dao sighed and raised his head.
Though the ceiling of the Buddha hall blocked his view, the old monk’s profound gaze seemed to pierce straight through it.
“The heavenly patterns are becoming distorted. Drawing closer, and moving faster.”
“Then, amid all that, a Morning Star rose. Even in those chaotic heavens, its light was unmistakably clear.”
Jeok Cheongang’s eyelids trembled.
“And?”
Hong Dao considered the question for a long moment, then shook his head.
“That is all I can say. Though the heavenly patterns are in turmoil, they still retain their form, and the great trees rooted throughout the realm will not be easily shaken. However...”
An inscrutable light entered Hong Dao’s eyes.

The words that followed carried the wisdom of a sage—of the current Abbot of Shaolin, the sect hailed for a thousand years as the Mount Tai and Northern Dipper of the Murim, and of a man deeply versed in the study of the heavens.
“An unknown calamity is approaching. Dark clouds will roll in from somewhere, covering the sun and swallowing the stars.”
A sky steeped in darkness, without a single ray of light.
Imagining it, Jeok Cheongang let one word slip out like a groan.
“Dark Heaven?”
“Dark Heaven. Yes, it will become just as you said—”
Jeok Cheongang hastily cut him off.
“No, that’s not what I meant. I remembered something Jin Wikyung, the Lesser Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, told me.”
“Jin Wikyung? I don’t know who that is, but are you saying he predicted this situation as well?”
“More accurately, it appeared before them. I saw it with my own eyes.”
Jeok Cheongang gave Hong Dao a detailed account of what had happened seven days and nights earlier, just before he left the Jin Family of Taiyuan.

He told him about the surviving remnants of the Head Elder’s faction, who were still alive despite the restrictions placed on them, and about everything that had happened up to that point. He also told him about the mysterious pill called the Temporary Strength Pill that he had taken from Pung Yang, the Red Wind Band Leader.
Jin Wikyung had passed all those facts to Jeok Cheongang, and Jeok Cheongang now passed them to Hong Dao.
“It was astonishing. The restrictions placed on them were so complex that even I couldn’t easily break them, and the effects of that Temporary Strength Pill were bizarrely powerful.”
“To think such a thing happened...”
“The hidden force that manipulated the Blade of Flowers from the shadows for decades. They are Dark Heaven.”
When the story ended, Hong Dao let out a low groan and sank into thought.
A long time passed before he finally spoke.
“Leave immediately.”
“It seems the time has come for each of us to do what we must. I will devote all my strength to preparing for this calamity, and you...”
Jeok Cheongang gazed deeply at his old friend and finished the sentence.
“You must stay beside the Morning Star. So it doesn’t fade easily.”
Jeok Cheongang knew his task did not end there. He had to protect that light while helping it shine even brighter.
Having realized their respective duties, neither man hesitated any longer.
“I’ll be going.”
“I won’t see you off. We’ll save the rest of our reunion for another time.”
Their separation had been long, and their reunion short.
Jeok Cheongang smiled at Hong Dao one last time, then strode out of the Buddha hall without hesitation.
Remembering the words he had not managed to finish saying.
It was a short meeting, but I enjoyed it.
Late that night, the young man and the old man left Shaoshi Peak on Mount Song.
They continued walking until the sun rose and set once more.

sentences.text: Unlike the short Jeok Cheongang, Dharma King Hong Dao was a remarkably tall old man.
His eyes sparkled with mischief, and his steps were full of vigor as he climbed the mountain path.
Where are we going, anyway?
It was only natural to wonder.
He had abandoned the well-maintained road and was deliberately taking paths hardly anyone ever used.
After walking for some time, Hong Dao finally stopped.
“Humble guests have come to this precious place.
I know it may be a burden, but don’t stand on ceremony.
Come in.”
Jeok Cheongang stared at the so-called precious place before speaking.
“Did you get kicked out of Shaolin Temple or something?”
“Hm?
Why?”
“You really have to ask?
What happened to your residence?”
Just as Jeok Cheongang had said, the place was surrounded by thick weeds and trees.
It looked far too shabby to be the residence of the Abbot of Shaolin Temple, the Mount Tai and Northern Dipper of the Murim.
“Be honest.
You got fired as Abbot of Shaolin, didn’t you?”
Seriously, what was he, a convenience-store part-timer?
Dumbfounded by Jeok Cheongang’s words, I asked, “Can an Abbot even be fired?”
“What a narrow-minded fool.
Rebels can depose an emperor, so why couldn’t they do the same to an Abbot of Shaolin?”
When he put it that way, I had nothing to say.
Besides, I used to beat monsters for a living in the modern world.
In a world with Demon Kings and Gates, I supposed even the Abbot of Shaolin could be a temporary employee.
Hong Dao, who had been listening to our exchange, chuckled.
“Wherever I am becomes the Abbot’s quarters.
We don’t bother with such formalities at Shaolin.
Isn’t that right, Disciple?”
Unnamed answered, “He is currently staying here despite the Discipline Hall’s pleas for him to return.”
Like friend, like friend.
This old man was no pushover either.
Hong Dao, however, only laughed heartily as he pulled out some kind of staff from inside his robes and waved it around.
“What can they do?
They’re the ones who forced the position of Abbot on someone who said he didn’t want it.”
It was a ridiculously short staff.
Its surface, polished by countless hands, gleamed as though it had been oiled, and a faint green light shimmered across it.
And there’s some strange-looking stone set into it.
Its shape somewhat resembled the staffs used by mages.
But there was something different about Hong Dao’s green staff.
Beyond the marks left by time, it possessed a unique energy all its own.
What is that?
My question was answered the next moment.
“The Green Jade Buddha Staff.
To think they entrusted a thousand-year-old sacred treasure of Shaolin, one bearing such immense authority, to a dirty monk like this.
They must all be blind.”
Jeok Cheongang clicked his tongue.
“Shaolin is really going downhill.”
“It’s still doing much better than the Fire Gate Clan, which has all of one Disciple.”
“What did you say?”
“Your fiery temper hasn’t changed.
I hope you’re reborn as a good and calm person in your next life.”
“My next life?
Why are you killing me off when I’m still perfectly healthy?”
“Oh, my.
A corpse is talking.
Amitabha.”
“Hong Dao, you dirty monk!”
I watched the two of them bicker as they entered the Buddha hall, then turned around.
Unnamed was looking at me with a faint smile.
“They both seem pleased to see an old friend after so long.”
“...I can’t imagine how they ever became friends.”
The eccentric Abbot of Shaolin and the foul-tempered Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan.
Their personalities might be a decent match, but they still didn’t seem like the sort of pair who would become friends.
Besides, hadn’t Jeok Cheongang killed countless people, despite Buddhism’s prohibition against taking life?
Unnamed thought over my dubious remark, then suddenly smacked his gleaming forehead.
“Ah, I remember now.”
“You startled me.
I thought you were about to use Solar Fist...
But what did you remember?”
“How they became friends.
During the Great Faction War, my master was secretly drinking and eating meat.
Benefactor Jeok caught him, and they became drinking buddies afterward.”
“What?”
For a moment, I wondered if I had misheard him.
“He was drinking and eating meat?”
“Yes.”
“Wasn’t he already the Abbot of Shaolin back then?”
“That is correct.”
“Oh, so the monks here eat meat.
Well, I suppose they need to bulk up while training in martial arts, so that makes sense...”
“That is not the case.
Buddhism forbids taking life.
Livestock are no exception.”
Where had this conversation gone wrong?
I stared blankly at Unnamed for a while, unable to say anything more.
Then I looked at the muscles writhing beneath his loose robes and became certain.
This bastard eats meat too.
Just look at those muscles.
There was no way he had built a physique like that on temple vegetable bibimbap alone.
He would have to roast an entire pig whenever he got bored, and even his bibimbap would have to be beef-tartare bibimbap.
Shaolin Temple?
More like the Temple of Wine Pools and Meat Forests.
Whoever said you couldn’t predict even an inch ahead in the Murim had been absolutely right.
Shaking my head, I followed the others into the Buddha hall.
The interior of the Buddha hall was small and old, but it had an elegant, antique charm.
The floor was spotless, and Buddha statues of every size stood throughout the hall.
Unnamed stepped away for a while, leaving Jeok Cheongang, Hong Dao, and me seated across from one another, emptying our teacups.
The tea, brewed from some unknown herb, was bitter and astringent.
“This is no way to treat an honored guest.
What is this?”
“What do you think?
Tea leaves I grew myself.”
“Tea leaves?
You?”
“I’m old enough to know better, so I decided it was time to give up ‘grain tea’ as well.
That was decades ago.”
For someone who had supposedly given it up, he seemed to have drunk enough alcohol to last a lifetime.
I couldn’t bring myself to say it aloud and merely tipped my cup back.
Jeok Cheongang, on the other hand, gaped at him.
“Are you sick?
Do you have some terminal disease?”
“A terminal disease...
Perhaps I do, perhaps I don’t.
I’m not sure myself.”
His answer was calm, but Jeok Cheongang’s face stiffened.
“Does that mean...?”
“We’ll discuss that later.”
Hong Dao lightly waved a hand to cut him off, then turned and stared intently at me.
“Now, then...
Are you the Master of Morning Star?”
The Master of Morning Star.
I had first heard the phrase from Unnamed only half a day ago.
I assumed rumors about a Morning Star appearing in the Murim had spread through the usual gossip.
The rumor has already reached this far?
The name Sleeping Dragon of Shanxi was gaining popularity by the day, but I hadn’t expected even the Abbot of Shaolin to recognize me.
Having suddenly gone world-class, I smiled awkwardly.
“That’s too much praise.
I’m not quite at that level yet.”
“You’re more obtuse than you look.”
“Excuse me?”
“Did I not call you the Master of Morning Star?”
Yes, but what does that mean?
Seeing my bewildered expression, Hong Dao smiled faintly.
“Benefactor, do you know what a Morning Star is?”
“Uh, well...
Don’t people usually call those who distinguish themselves Morning Stars?”
“And?”
“...A star?”
“Exactly.”
Hong Dao nodded and continued in a calm voice.
“I have observed the heavens for a very long time.
Perhaps the effort was not entirely futile, for I eventually learned to see and read the heavenly patterns to some extent.”
“The heavenly patterns...”
The events of the past half day suddenly flashed through my mind.
Unnamed had come looking for us on his master’s orders, and the moment he saw me, he had called me the Master of Morning Star.
And what had Jeok Cheongang said?
Ah, right.
What an uncanny dirty monk.
He can still see a thousand ri without leaving his seat.
He hadn’t guided us here using information gathered from other people.
He had read the heavenly patterns.
If that’s true, he’s far beyond some fake fortune-teller.
Calling it prophecy wouldn’t even be an exaggeration.
I sensed something unusual from Hong Dao and swallowed hard.
“So?”
“A Morning Star is like a firework.
It shines brightly in the night sky, then fades with time.
But this one was different.”
Hong Dao pointed through the open doors of the Buddha hall, toward the distant north where Shanxi Province lay.
“One day, a new Morning Star rose in the north.
Its light has yet to fade.
No, it grows brighter with each passing day.”
“People often compare humans to stars.
I believe that Morning Star is you.”
Whenever someone is born or dies after accomplishing something great, people rejoice or lament.
A new star has risen.
Or a great star has fallen.
But the Morning Star that appeared this time is supposed to be me?
Hong Dao clearly meant it as something good.
Still, I wasn’t sure what to make of it.
Just as I scratched the back of my head with a perplexed expression, one of Hong Dao’s words pierced my ears.
“That was four months ago.”
My entire body tingled as though I had been struck by electricity.
My mouth went dry, and my heart pounded.
One thought spun endlessly through my mind.
Four months ago?
If it was then...
That was around the time I had first awakened in the Murim.
Hong Dao smiled warmly at me as I swallowed dryly.
“You seem to have something in mind.”
“N-no.
Nothing at all.”
Jeok Cheongang, who had been listening silently, cut in with a disgusted look.
“It’s written all over your face, you idiot.”
“I-it really isn’t.”
“Oh?
Shall I rip out that tongue of yours?”
“W-why are you doing this to me?”
Damn it.
My tongue wouldn’t stop tripping over itself.
Hong Dao burst into laughter as I slowly edged my bottom away from Jeok Cheongang to avoid his sharp gaze.
“It seems the benefactor is in urgent need of the privy.
You may leave.”
“Go on—if you want me to shove you into the latrine.”
I looked back and forth between the two of them, then bolted for the door.
Behind me, I heard Hong Dao’s booming laughter and Jeok Cheongang’s shouts.
“Ha!
Ha-ha-ha!”
“What an ill-mannered brat.
How dare he run off while his master is speaking...”
Hong Dao looked at the grumbling Jeok Cheongang.
“Is he the Disciple you recently took in?”
Jeok Cheongang flinched and hurriedly cleared his throat.
“Ahem.
Kheh-hem!
He isn’t my Disciple.
He begged and pleaded for me to teach him a thing or two, so I’m merely looking after him for a while.
Yes.
That’s all.”
“Is that so?”
“I told you it is!”
“If that’s the case, why are you shouting?
You’ll anger the Buddhas.”
“Hah.
Listen to the way this dirty monk talks.”
Ignoring Jeok Cheongang’s reaction, Hong Dao drained his teacup in one gulp and grimaced.
“Ugh, bitter.
Hurry and finish yours.”
“Finish this crap?
Why would I drink something so bitter?”
“How can I pour the liquor if your cup isn’t empty?”
“What?”
“I’ve been saving something for a day like this.”
With a sly smile thoroughly unbecoming of a monk, Hong Dao rose and approached the row of Buddha statues.
He effortlessly lifted aside the largest statue, fumbled behind it, and pulled out a small earthenware jar.
“Snake liquor aged for thirty years.”
“Snake liquor?”
“The Thousand-Year Poison Horned Snake.
Have you heard of it?”
“The Thousand-Year Poison Horned Snake!”
Jeok Cheongang’s eyes lit up.
He hurriedly opened the tightly sealed jar.
Sure enough, the snake inside was larger than a python, with a horn protruding from its triangular head.
A poisonous aura strong enough to make his nose tingle poured from the jar.
Jeok Cheongang stared in amazement.
“Isn’t this thing lethally venomous?
Where did you catch it?”
Hong Dao gazed off toward the distant mountains.
“While I was out for a walk.”
“...You must have searched the whole mountain with the intention of making snake liquor from the start.
There are limits to being a dirty monk.
Now you’re killing things just to have a drink?”
“If you don’t want any, never mind.
I’ll drink it myself.”
“Now, now.”
Jeok Cheongang gave Hong Dao a pointed glare, then muttered, “Still, this thing’s venom must be no joke...”
“Indeed.
A single drop of venom squeezed from a Thousand-Year Poison Horned Snake can kill a hundred cows.”
“It’s been in there for thirty years.
At this point, that’s not liquor.
It’s poison.”
“We only broke the seal for a moment, and already this much poisonous energy has spread through the air.
What more is there to say?”
“Something this strong would kill even a decent master, wouldn’t it?”
“It would be madness to drink it.
We absolutely shouldn’t.”
Their gazes met in midair.
Then they spoke almost simultaneously.
“Then we have to drink it.”
“Of course.
Absolutely.”
“Surely it won’t kill us.”
“Drink.
We’re drinking it no matter what.
I read the heavenly patterns, and today isn’t the day we die.”
Both men were over a hundred years old, yet neither could escape the simple recklessness etched deep into every man’s bones.
Before long, they were passing the jar back and forth and guzzling the liquor as though possessed.
Half a shichen later, early darkness had settled over the mountain, and the jar was empty.
“Ooh, that venomous tingle on the tip of the tongue gives it an incredible kick.
Thanks to my Scorching Yang Qi, the poison can’t even touch me.”
Jeok Cheongang licked up the very last drop while Hong Dao glared at him.
Though both men numbered among the Ten Kings, a slight difference in skill still existed.
Hong Dao had lost out in the grappling technique they used to wrestle the jar away from each other, so he had not managed to drink even half of what it contained.
“An old brute with nothing but strength.
No wonder you’ve lived so long.”
“Were you hoping I’d die?”
“I at least expected you to clutch your stomach and roll around.”
Pleasantly drunk, Jeok Cheongang burst into laughter.
“That’s what the heavenly patterns said, isn’t it?
What can you do when Heaven has decided your lifespan?”
“The heavenly patterns...”
Hong Dao murmured the words, then casually added, “That was a lie.”
“Hm?
What do you mean?”
“Exactly what I said.
I’ve been slowly going blind for the past thirty years.”
“W-wait.
Are you saying you can no longer read the heavenly patterns?”
Hong Dao nodded silently, and Jeok Cheongang’s heart sank.
“How did it happen?
Is it because of your age?”
“At first, I thought so too.
But I was mistaken.
I gave up the liquor I loved so much and secluded myself in the wilderness to calm my mind, yet nothing changed.”
“Then...”
“It isn’t because this old man’s faculties have grown dull.”
Hong Dao sighed and raised his head.
Though the ceiling of the Buddha hall blocked his view, the old monk’s profound gaze seemed to pierce straight through it.
“The heavenly patterns are becoming distorted.
Drawing closer, and moving faster.”
“Then, amid all that, a Morning Star rose.
Even in those chaotic heavens, its light was unmistakably clear.”
Jeok Cheongang’s eyelids trembled.
“And?”
Hong Dao considered the question for a long moment, then shook his head.
“That is all I can say.
Though the heavenly patterns are in turmoil, they still retain their form, and the great trees rooted throughout the realm will not be easily shaken.
However...”
An inscrutable light entered Hong Dao’s eyes.

The words that followed carried the wisdom of a sage—of the current Abbot of Shaolin, the sect hailed for a thousand years as the Mount Tai and Northern Dipper of the Murim, and of a man deeply versed in the study of the heavens.
“An unknown calamity is approaching.
Dark clouds will roll in from somewhere, covering the sun and swallowing the stars.”
A sky steeped in darkness, without a single ray of light.
Imagining it, Jeok Cheongang let one word slip out like a groan.
“Dark Heaven?”
“Dark Heaven.
Yes, it will become just as you said—”
Jeok Cheongang hastily cut him off.
“No, that’s not what I meant.
I remembered something Jin Wikyung, the Lesser Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, told me.”
“Jin Wikyung?
I don’t know who that is, but are you saying he predicted this situation as well?”
“More accurately, it appeared before them.
I saw it with my own eyes.”
Jeok Cheongang gave Hong Dao a detailed account of what had happened seven days and nights earlier, just before he left the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
He told him about the surviving remnants of the Head Elder’s faction, who were still alive despite the restrictions placed on them, and about everything that had happened up to that point.
He also told him about the mysterious pill called the Temporary Strength Pill that he had taken from Pung Yang, the Red Wind Band Leader.
Jin Wikyung had passed all those facts to Jeok Cheongang, and Jeok Cheongang now passed them to Hong Dao.
“It was astonishing.
The restrictions placed on them were so complex that even I couldn’t easily break them, and the effects of that Temporary Strength Pill were bizarrely powerful.”
“To think such a thing happened...”
“The hidden force that manipulated the Blade of Flowers from the shadows for decades.
They are Dark Heaven.”
When the story ended, Hong Dao let out a low groan and sank into thought.
A long time passed before he finally spoke.
“Leave immediately.”
“It seems the time has come for each of us to do what we must.
I will devote all my strength to preparing for this calamity, and you...”
Jeok Cheongang gazed deeply at his old friend and finished the sentence.
“You must stay beside the Morning Star.
So it doesn’t fade easily.”
Jeok Cheongang knew his task did not end there.
He had to protect that light while helping it shine even brighter.
Having realized their respective duties, neither man hesitated any longer.
“I’ll be going.”
“I won’t see you off.
We’ll save the rest of our reunion for another time.”
Their separation had been long, and their reunion short.
Jeok Cheongang smiled at Hong Dao one last time, then strode out of the Buddha hall without hesitation.
Remembering the words he had not managed to finish saying.
It was a short meeting, but I enjoyed it.
Late that night, the young man and the old man left Shaoshi Peak on Mount Song.
They continued walking until the sun rose and set once more.

chapters.title: Chapter 233
paragraphs: The middle-aged man gazed down at the crystal-clear blade.
Blade-sharp features and tightly pressed lips stared back at him. Strands of white had begun to appear here and there in his reflected hair.
After a while, he suddenly spoke.
“You’ve had a long wait.”
His low but powerful voice echoed through the spacious room. Yet no one stood anywhere within sight.
The answer came from the ceiling above his head.
“It is my duty.”

The whisper belonged to the person known as the Hidden Thread. There had been a Hidden Thread in the previous generation, and the generation before that. The position had existed for hundreds of years, ever since the family was founded.
Sworn to absolute loyalty toward one person alone—the Family Head—they were, true to their name, threads hidden from sight.
The countless pieces of information that flowed along those threads could be quietly forgotten—or turned into weapons with which to strangle someone.
“Do you have any new information?”
“Yes. Heaven-grade.”
“Heaven-grade.”
The middle-aged man ran a finger along the blade.
Every report the Hidden Thread delivered was confidential, but they were divided by importance into Heaven, Earth, and Human grades.
Heaven-grade was the highest of them all.
Even for a man who had led his family for nearly twenty years, such reports were exceedingly rare.
“It has been a while. Is this the first since the Huangshan Sect?”
The Huangshan Sect was a prestigious sect with a long history. Yet now, its name was slowly fading from the memories of the people.
Survival of the fittest.
The Murim was a merciless world that did not look back at those who had been weeded out. The middle-aged man had weeded out the Huangshan Sect and feasted on their corpses.
“There should still be a long time left before they reopen their gates.”
“The Huangshan Sect has already collapsed. Even if it reopened its gates, it could never recover.”
“Then?”
“The Mountain Lord has returned.”
The fingers caressing the blade abruptly stopped.
“...Is that true?”
“Without a doubt.”
The Mountain Lord—the master of the mountain.
Some might wonder what sort of nonsense that was. There were countless mountains under heaven, so what sense did it make to speak of their owner?
But here in Anhui Province, the title Mountain Lord referred to only one man.
“Fire King Jeok Cheongang...”
An unparalleled master who had faced a thousand martial artists alone.
Mount Jiuhua was his domain and the sacred ground of the Fire Gate Clan, whose legacy stretched back hundreds of years.
On the day the Demonic Cultists set fire to Mount Jiuhua, an old man who had been aging like any other became the Fire King.
The people of Anhui Province, who had protected their precious home thanks to him, began calling him the Mountain Lord out of respect.
“When and where did the report come from?”
“He passed through the North Gate two shichen ago.”
“His destination?”
“Mount Jiuhua.”
“I see.”
The middle-aged man nodded slightly, then sensed something odd.
Since becoming Family Head, he had received countless reports from the Hidden Thread and asked for his assessments, but the man had never once spoken with such certainty.
This time was different.
Sensing his lord’s question, the Hidden Thread spoke first.
“He was accompanied by his Disciple. Going to his sect is only natural.”
“His Disciple?”
The middle-aged man frowned. The Fire Gate Clan passed its teachings from one master to a single Disciple. The Fire King could have only one.
Though it had happened nearly twenty years ago, he clearly remembered everything concerning the Fire King.
“Did he come back for that vicious bastard?”
“It is not the man you are thinking of. According to confirmed reports, he died three months ago.”
“And the Fire King found a new Disciple?”
“Yes.”
The Hidden Thread’s flat voice continued.
“Jin Taekyung. He turned twenty-one this year and belongs to the direct line of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
“Both the name and the family are unfamiliar to me.”

“He shares a bloodline with the Blade of Flowers, who distinguished himself during the Great Faction War, and the Heaven Shaking Sword, who has recently risen to prominence as one of the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes.”
“Ah, that Jin Family.”
“Yes.”
Fortunately, the two names given by the Hidden Thread were familiar enough to the middle-aged man.
“Hmm. So that is how it is.”
He sank into thought, forgetting even the Hidden Thread’s presence.
Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan. Fire King Jeok Cheongang’s new Disciple. No matter how much he considered it, the name remained unfamiliar.
But now he would have to become accustomed to it.
The Fire King chose a descendant of a frontier martial family.
He would never have accepted a man already past twenty as his new Disciple without good reason.
It must be one of two things. Either he has some leverage over the Fire King, or his martial talent is so extraordinary that his age and background are irrelevant.
The longer he considered it, the clearer the answer became.
A considerable amount of time had passed by the time he spoke again.
“Set every Lesser Thread in motion.”
The Lesser Threads were the countless informants serving beneath the Hidden Thread.
They gathered information from all across the realm, which flowed through the Hidden Thread before reaching the middle-aged man.
“Every one of them?”
For the first time, a faint trace of surprise entered the Hidden Thread’s voice.
The order meant focusing most of the family’s intelligence network on a single person.
But his surprise lasted only a moment. Remembering his duty, the Hidden Thread quickly answered.
“Forgive my insolence.”
“It doesn’t matter. I’ll give you a month. Use whatever means necessary and learn everything there is to know about that Disciple.”
“As you command.”
“You’ll be busy for a while.”
The Hidden Thread grasped the meaning behind those words, and his presence vanished as though it had been wiped clean.
His concealment technique had reached the very limits of the Peak realm. He would spend the next fortnight without a moment to breathe.
I can’t sit idle either.
The middle-aged man slowly rose.
Unlike his father, who had been a martial artist to the bone, he had been born to lead.
He had guided the family since his days as Lesser Family Head, cementing its position as a dominant power. Authority radiated from his entire bearing.
Step. Step. Step.
He crossed the spacious room in long strides and threw open the doors. The dozen or so guards surrounding the pavilion dropped to one knee in greeting.
“We greet the Family Head!”
The middle-aged man nodded slightly. Every one of them was an outstanding Peak swordsman and a blood relative who shared his lineage.
They were a vast clan united beneath the surname Namgung—a great tree rooted deep in the Murim.
“Gather the clan. The weather is fine, so we should all share a drink.”
“As you command!”
The middle-aged man, Namgung Ryong, raised his head toward the sky.
The boundless azure heaven stretched above him, not a single cloud in sight.
I spoke with the most solemn expression I could muster.
“I have a wish I’ve cherished for a long time.”
Jeok Cheongang answered in an equally grave voice.
“This old man has a wish as well.”
“If it wouldn’t be too rude, may I go first?”
“That would be extremely rude.”
“Then I’ll be rude just this once.”
“Want to have an accident in your pants? Should I make you piss and shit yourself for the rest of your life, not just this once?”
My mother would have been devastated if she had seen this.
I could have cried at how unfair it was, but I held back my tears and tried again.
“Please hear me out just once.”
“Fine. I know exactly what you’re after, but I’ll hear you out once.”
I swallowed dryly and stated my wish.
“Could we stop at an inn just once?”
“That’s your wish?”
“Yes.”
“Then this old man will tell you his.”
Jeok Cheongang glared at me with terrifying eyes.
“Shut your mouth and follow me.”
“Didn’t you say you wanted to train? We’re on our way to train, so what are you whining about?”
“When did I say I didn’t want to? I’m going to be stuck in the mountains for the next six months. All I’m asking is that we eat our fill and wash up once—just once—before that!”
My shout echoed through the darkened mountains.
That was right. We were standing at the foot of Mount Jiuhua in Anhui Province.
“It took seven days and nights to get from Shanxi Province to Henan, then another seven days and nights to get from Henan to Anhui. I haven’t even slept properly.”
At least before we reached Henan, he had let me sleep for a shichen at a time. After we left Hong Dao’s residence, however, he had shown me absolutely no mercy.
We ran and ran, chewing jerky without even stopping for meals.
“I wanted to eat Shaolin Temple’s wild-vegetable bibimbap!”
During the fifteen-day forced march, the only proper meal I’d had was at the inn in Luoyang.
“And even then, you ate all the drumsticks! You left me one wing and nothing but dry breast meat!”
I had barely gotten to tear off a few pieces of meat when some sword-wielding dark-path figures showed up and ruined everything. Then the Under Armour monk appeared and took me to Shaolin Temple.
“I kept asking you to stop at an inn. What did you say? That we were almost there. That we could rest when we arrived!”
“And here we are. Mount Jiuhua.”
Jeok Cheongang dug into his ear with a grimy pinky nail, then blew the earwax away.
“Go up and rest. Once we’re there, you can eat your fill, wash, and sleep.”
“Eating my fill just means jerky and fasting pills. Forget hot water—I’ll get nothing but a nonstop forest bath. And you won’t even let me sleep for half a shichen a day!”
“Hahaha!”
Jeok Cheongang laughed heartily, then stopped dead. At the same time, a chilling energy seeped from his entire body.
“This is why I don’t like youngsters with sharp instincts.”
Big Brother Ed...
Wait, no.
Goose bumps raced down my spine.
His voice came out cold as ice.
“Yes, you guessed correctly. I intend to let you sleep for half a shichen a day and work you like a dog.”
“Gasp!”

“I’ll use fasting pills to squeeze every last drop of fat from your body. Then, for six months straight, I’ll put you through the most extreme training humanly imaginable, without missing a single day.”
“Y-you devil.”
“Did you just call this old man a demon? I suppose I’ll have to make your training even harder.”
“N-no. This is a scam.”
“Why don’t you understand that by the time you realize that, it’s already too late?”
“Wait. I need to visit the privy for a moment.”
As I slowly backed away, the Fire King extended a wrinkled palm toward me.
“You came of your own free will, but leaving isn’t up to you.”
Whoosh!
An overwhelming force I had never felt before became ropes that bound my entire body.
Neither my near-superhuman physical abilities nor my nearly one jiazi of internal energy could do a thing.
I tried to resist somehow, but it was already too late. Following the movement of his hand, my body floated into the air.
“Seizing an Object Through Empty Space?”
“If you recognize it, hurry over.”
Whoosh!
The next moment, I shot toward Jeok Cheongang faster than an arrow. At the same time, one of his wrinkled fingers brushed a spot on my neck.
A sharp sting was followed by an ominous sound in my ear.
Beep!
System You have been struck by Pressure-Point Strike! Your Sleep Acupoint has been struck. You cannot resist sleep! 5 seconds, 4 seconds, 3 seconds, 2 seconds...
Drowsiness swept over me with the System’s countdown.
As my consciousness blurred, Jeok Cheongang’s voice slowly receded into the distance.
“Today, I’ll make a special exception and let you sleep for two shichen.”
Well, fuck. How very generous.
I couldn’t force the words from the tip of my tongue before sleep claimed me.
Snore. Snore.
“That young bastard is absurdly strong.”
Jeok Cheongang clicked his tongue as he looked down at the peacefully sleeping Jin Taekyung.
Seizing an Object Through Empty Space and Pressure-Point Strike were not omnipotent. The amount of force they required varied depending on the opponent.
It was a good thing he had known what kind of person this young man was. If he had been caught off guard and his technique had been countered, he would have been utterly humiliated.
“It feels like only yesterday that I met him in Shanxi, yet he has already come this far... What a strange fellow.”
Just as Jeok Cheongang let out a weary sigh, his vision suddenly blurred and the strength drained from his legs.
“Gasp!”
Thud.
He barely managed to regain his senses before grabbing hold of a nearby tree.
His heart pounded, and his mind snapped fully awake as though someone had dumped cold water over him in his sleep.
“Th-this...”
Had he expended too much strength at once? Or had his aged body failed to withstand the arduous journey?
Jeok Cheongang bit his lip. Although his prime as a martial artist had passed, he was still a Supreme Peak master who had reached the pinnacle of martial arts.
It wasn’t his body that had grown old. It was something else.
I must hurry. I don’t have much time.
Perhaps that was why his old friend Hong Dao had told him to leave immediately.
After steadying himself, Jeok Cheongang slung Jin Taekyung over his back. Though he was more than a hundred years old, the young man’s massive frame felt as light as a feather.
“Not yet. It can’t happen yet.”
He muttered in a voice that had suddenly grown much older, then set off.
More than ten jang vanished beneath each step, and the scenery flashed past.
Before long, thick fog rolled in and erased every trace of him.

sentences.text: The middle-aged man gazed down at the crystal-clear blade.
Blade-sharp features and tightly pressed lips stared back at him.
Strands of white had begun to appear here and there in his reflected hair.
After a while, he suddenly spoke.
“You’ve had a long wait.”
His low but powerful voice echoed through the spacious room.
Yet no one stood anywhere within sight.
The answer came from the ceiling above his head.
“It is my duty.”
The whisper belonged to the person known as the Hidden Thread.
There had been a Hidden Thread in the previous generation, and the generation before that.
The position had existed for hundreds of years, ever since the family was founded.
Sworn to absolute loyalty toward one person alone—the Family Head—they were, true to their name, threads hidden from sight.
The countless pieces of information that flowed along those threads could be quietly forgotten—or turned into weapons with which to strangle someone.
“Do you have any new information?”
“Yes.
Heaven-grade.”
“Heaven-grade.”
The middle-aged man ran a finger along the blade.
Every report the Hidden Thread delivered was confidential, but they were divided by importance into Heaven, Earth, and Human grades.
Heaven-grade was the highest of them all.
Even for a man who had led his family for nearly twenty years, such reports were exceedingly rare.
“It has been a while.
Is this the first since the Huangshan Sect?”
The Huangshan Sect was a prestigious sect with a long history.
Yet now, its name was slowly fading from the memories of the people.
Survival of the fittest.
The Murim was a merciless world that did not look back at those who had been weeded out.
The middle-aged man had weeded out the Huangshan Sect and feasted on their corpses.
“There should still be a long time left before they reopen their gates.”
“The Huangshan Sect has already collapsed.
Even if it reopened its gates, it could never recover.”
“Then?”
“The Mountain Lord has returned.”
The fingers caressing the blade abruptly stopped.
“...Is that true?”
“Without a doubt.”
The Mountain Lord—the master of the mountain.
Some might wonder what sort of nonsense that was.
There were countless mountains under heaven, so what sense did it make to speak of their owner?
But here in Anhui Province, the title Mountain Lord referred to only one man.
“Fire King Jeok Cheongang...”
An unparalleled master who had faced a thousand martial artists alone.
Mount Jiuhua was his domain and the sacred ground of the Fire Gate Clan, whose legacy stretched back hundreds of years.
On the day the Demonic Cultists set fire to Mount Jiuhua, an old man who had been aging like any other became the Fire King.
The people of Anhui Province, who had protected their precious home thanks to him, began calling him the Mountain Lord out of respect.
“When and where did the report come from?”
“He passed through the North Gate two shichen ago.”
“His destination?”
“Mount Jiuhua.”
“I see.”
The middle-aged man nodded slightly, then sensed something odd.
Since becoming Family Head, he had received countless reports from the Hidden Thread and asked for his assessments, but the man had never once spoken with such certainty.
This time was different.
Sensing his lord’s question, the Hidden Thread spoke first.
“He was accompanied by his Disciple.
Going to his sect is only natural.”
“His Disciple?”
The middle-aged man frowned.
The Fire Gate Clan passed its teachings from one master to a single Disciple.
The Fire King could have only one.
Though it had happened nearly twenty years ago, he clearly remembered everything concerning the Fire King.
“Did he come back for that vicious bastard?”
“It is not the man you are thinking of.
According to confirmed reports, he died three months ago.”
“And the Fire King found a new Disciple?”
“Yes.”
The Hidden Thread’s flat voice continued.
“Jin Taekyung.
He turned twenty-one this year and belongs to the direct line of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
“Both the name and the family are unfamiliar to me.”

“He shares a bloodline with the Blade of Flowers, who distinguished himself during the Great Faction War, and the Heaven Shaking Sword, who has recently risen to prominence as one of the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes.”
“Ah, that Jin Family.”
“Yes.”
Fortunately, the two names given by the Hidden Thread were familiar enough to the middle-aged man.
“Hmm.
So that is how it is.”
He sank into thought, forgetting even the Hidden Thread’s presence.
Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Fire King Jeok Cheongang’s new Disciple.
No matter how much he considered it, the name remained unfamiliar.
But now he would have to become accustomed to it.
The Fire King chose a descendant of a frontier martial family.
He would never have accepted a man already past twenty as his new Disciple without good reason.
It must be one of two things.
Either he has some leverage over the Fire King, or his martial talent is so extraordinary that his age and background are irrelevant.
The longer he considered it, the clearer the answer became.
A considerable amount of time had passed by the time he spoke again.
“Set every Lesser Thread in motion.”
The Lesser Threads were the countless informants serving beneath the Hidden Thread.
They gathered information from all across the realm, which flowed through the Hidden Thread before reaching the middle-aged man.
“Every one of them?”
For the first time, a faint trace of surprise entered the Hidden Thread’s voice.
The order meant focusing most of the family’s intelligence network on a single person.
But his surprise lasted only a moment.
Remembering his duty, the Hidden Thread quickly answered.
“Forgive my insolence.”
“It doesn’t matter.
I’ll give you a month.
Use whatever means necessary and learn everything there is to know about that Disciple.”
“As you command.”
“You’ll be busy for a while.”
The Hidden Thread grasped the meaning behind those words, and his presence vanished as though it had been wiped clean.
His concealment technique had reached the very limits of the Peak realm.
He would spend the next fortnight without a moment to breathe.
I can’t sit idle either.
The middle-aged man slowly rose.
Unlike his father, who had been a martial artist to the bone, he had been born to lead.
He had guided the family since his days as Lesser Family Head, cementing its position as a dominant power.
Authority radiated from his entire bearing.
Step.
Step.
Step.
He crossed the spacious room in long strides and threw open the doors.
The dozen or so guards surrounding the pavilion dropped to one knee in greeting.
“We greet the Family Head!”
The middle-aged man nodded slightly.
Every one of them was an outstanding Peak swordsman and a blood relative who shared his lineage.
They were a vast clan united beneath the surname Namgung—a great tree rooted deep in the Murim.
“Gather the clan.
The weather is fine, so we should all share a drink.”
“As you command!”
The middle-aged man, Namgung Ryong, raised his head toward the sky.
The boundless azure heaven stretched above him, not a single cloud in sight.
I spoke with the most solemn expression I could muster.
“I have a wish I’ve cherished for a long time.”
Jeok Cheongang answered in an equally grave voice.
“This old man has a wish as well.”
“If it wouldn’t be too rude, may I go first?”
“That would be extremely rude.”
“Then I’ll be rude just this once.”
“Want to have an accident in your pants?
Should I make you piss and shit yourself for the rest of your life, not just this once?”
My mother would have been devastated if she had seen this.
I could have cried at how unfair it was, but I held back my tears and tried again.
“Please hear me out just once.”
“Fine.
I know exactly what you’re after, but I’ll hear you out once.”
I swallowed dryly and stated my wish.
“Could we stop at an inn just once?”
“That’s your wish?”
“Yes.”
“Then this old man will tell you his.”
Jeok Cheongang glared at me with terrifying eyes.
“Shut your mouth and follow me.”
“Didn’t you say you wanted to train?
We’re on our way to train, so what are you whining about?”
“When did I say I didn’t want to?
I’m going to be stuck in the mountains for the next six months.
All I’m asking is that we eat our fill and wash up once—just once—before that!”
My shout echoed through the darkened mountains.
That was right.
We were standing at the foot of Mount Jiuhua in Anhui Province.
“It took seven days and nights to get from Shanxi Province to Henan, then another seven days and nights to get from Henan to Anhui.
I haven’t even slept properly.”
At least before we reached Henan, he had let me sleep for a shichen at a time.
After we left Hong Dao’s residence, however, he had shown me absolutely no mercy.
We ran and ran, chewing jerky without even stopping for meals.
“I wanted to eat Shaolin Temple’s wild-vegetable bibimbap!”
During the fifteen-day forced march, the only proper meal I’d had was at the inn in Luoyang.
“And even then, you ate all the drumsticks!
You left me one wing and nothing but dry breast meat!”
I had barely gotten to tear off a few pieces of meat when some sword-wielding dark-path figures showed up and ruined everything.
Then the Under Armour monk appeared and took me to Shaolin Temple.
“I kept asking you to stop at an inn.
What did you say?
That we were almost there.
That we could rest when we arrived!”
“And here we are.
Mount Jiuhua.”
Jeok Cheongang dug into his ear with a grimy pinky nail, then blew the earwax away.
“Go up and rest.
Once we’re there, you can eat your fill, wash, and sleep.”
“Eating my fill just means jerky and fasting pills.
Forget hot water—I’ll get nothing but a nonstop forest bath.
And you won’t even let me sleep for half a shichen a day!”
“Hahaha!”
Jeok Cheongang laughed heartily, then stopped dead.
At the same time, a chilling energy seeped from his entire body.
“This is why I don’t like youngsters with sharp instincts.”
Big Brother Ed...
Wait, no.
Goose bumps raced down my spine.
His voice came out cold as ice.
“Yes, you guessed correctly.
I intend to let you sleep for half a shichen a day and work you like a dog.”
“Gasp!”
“I’ll use fasting pills to squeeze every last drop of fat from your body.
Then, for six months straight, I’ll put you through the most extreme training humanly imaginable, without missing a single day.”
“Y-you devil.”
“Did you just call this old man a demon?
I suppose I’ll have to make your training even harder.”
“N-no.
This is a scam.”
“Why don’t you understand that by the time you realize that, it’s already too late?”
“Wait.
I need to visit the privy for a moment.”
As I slowly backed away, the Fire King extended a wrinkled palm toward me.
“You came of your own free will, but leaving isn’t up to you.”
Whoosh!
An overwhelming force I had never felt before became ropes that bound my entire body.
Neither my near-superhuman physical abilities nor my nearly one jiazi of internal energy could do a thing.
I tried to resist somehow, but it was already too late.
Following the movement of his hand, my body floated into the air.

Whoosh!
The next moment, I shot toward Jeok Cheongang faster than an arrow.

A sharp sting was followed by an ominous sound in my ear.
Beep!
